title: Charlie Parker and college kids waiting outside
summary: Five hundred students waited outside until Parker arrived after a Birdland set, while McRae outbid Birdland on fees.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Well anyway -- Because I remember that one night we had Charlie Parker on the bill. And all these kids came over from the school -- college kids came over. About five hundred and they stayed outside. They wasn't gonna go in until The Bird in. (inaudible). "We aint' going in until The Bird fly in."
The Bird flew in, then all -- Well it was about a dollar to get in -- that's all. Two dollars to get in, something like that.

And they stood out -- So Bird -- what Charlie did, instead of him coming up and doing my concert and go on back to -- he stopped down at the Birdland and did a whole concert with them, and told them he had to go to Newark to do a Concert In Jam. So that's the fellow found -- (inaudible), "What's going on in Newark, we got to go to Newark?" He say, "No, I got an engagement to go do the Concert In Jam." "Concert In Jam? Who's doing Con" -- That's when he found out that I was -- had a concert over in Newark, (inaudible) he had Birdland that night. Any Monday night he had a concert -- I had a show in Birdland over here in Newark that was killing the show in Birdland, because I had all the stars. Not only I had one, I had like two and three. They would go down there and then -- I was paying (inaudible) like Ben came up -- I think like a hundred and seventy-five dollars. I paid

Miles Davis a hundred and seventy-five or two hundred dollars just to come over and do one up. They weren't getting that kind of money at Birdland. They go down in Birdland and maybe Birdland give them seventy-five dollars or fifty dollars to do a show or something, like on a Monday night.
I was paying the guys good money, because I was making good money. And didn't mind. I say, "Well who you guys want?" They say we want so and so. Come on, you know.
This was around 1953 or something or '54?
